title: Rome's first sufficiency attack: lost canonical books would leave doctrine incomplete
source_text: II. Primum ergo, ut probent Scripturam non continere omnia quae ad fidem & religionem necessaria sunt, in hunc modum argumentantur. Si Scripturae omnia necessaria ad fidem & salutem sufficienter continerent, id intelligendum esset, vel de toto Scripturae Canone, qui simul sumptus sufficiens esset; vel de singulis Scripturae partibus, quae singulae per se sufficerent. At neutrum dici potest. Et quidem de singulis libris manifestum est eos seorsim sumptos, & absque reliquo Scripturae corpore non continere omnia necessaria ad salutem. Nec enim prophetia quaevis Veteris Testamenti, aut Novi Testamenti Epistola quaelibet omnia fidei dogmata complectitur. Restat ergo, ut illa perfectio & sufficientia toti Scripturae sacrae Canoni tribuenda sit. Itaque ut habeatur integra salutis doctrina, necesse est ut integer Scripturae Canon habeatur. Quod si aliquid desit in Scripturae Canone, in doctrina quoque aliquid deficere necesse est. Jam autem non habetur integer Scripturae Canon. Igitur ex Scriptura, prout illam hodie habemus, doctrina salutis non potest sufficienter hauriri. Quod autem nunc non habeatur integer Scripturae Canon inde probant quod multi libri sacri interciderunt, tam ex Veteri, quam ex Novo Testamento. Et ex Veteri quidem Testamento libri Nathan & Gad Videntis, de quibus mentio fit cap. ult. lib. 1. Paralip. Et libri item Ahiae Scilonitae & Addo Videntis, de quibus mentio fit 2. Paralip. 9. hodie non extant amplius. Ut nec quinquies mille Salomonis Cantica, & tria millia parabolarum quae loquutus fuisse dicitur 1 Reg. 4. Ex Novo vero Testamento aiunt periisse Epistolam ad Laodicenses, cujus mentio fit, ut putant, ult. cap. Epist. ad Colos. Et forte aliam quandam Epistolam ad Corinthios, cujus mentio fieri videtur 1 Cor. 5.
pass_a_gloss: First, then, to prove that Scripture does not contain all things necessary to faith and religion, they argue thus. If the Scriptures sufficiently contained all things necessary to faith and salvation, that would have to be understood either of the whole Canon of Scripture taken together as sufficient, or of the several parts of Scripture, each of which would suffice by itself. But neither can be said. And as to the several books, it is plain that taken separately, and without the rest of the body of Scripture, they do not contain all things necessary to salvation. For not every prophecy of the Old Testament, nor every Epistle of the New, embraces all the dogmas of faith. It remains, therefore, that that perfection and sufficiency must be ascribed to the whole sacred Scripture, to the Canon. So, for the complete doctrine of salvation to be had, the whole Canon of Scripture must be had. If anything is missing in the Canon of Scripture, something must also be missing in the doctrine. But now the whole Canon of Scripture is not had. Therefore from Scripture as we have it today the doctrine of salvation cannot be sufficiently drawn. That the whole Canon is not now had they prove from the fact that many sacred books have perished, both from the Old and from the New Testament: from the Old, the books of Nathan and Gad the Seer mentioned in the last chapter of 1 Chronicles, and likewise of Ahijah the Shilonite and Iddo the Seer mentioned in 2 Chronicles 9, which no longer exist; also Solomon's five thousand songs and three thousand parables spoken of in 1 Kings 4; from the New, they say the Epistle to the Laodiceans has perished, mentioned as they think in the last chapter of Colossians, and perhaps another Epistle to the Corinthians hinted at in 1 Cor. 5.
pass_b_english: Rome's opening move: if Scripture were enough, either the whole Canon together would be enough, or each book by itself would be enough.
Neither works. Single books, cut off from the rest, do not hold every saving dogma — not every OT prophecy, not every NT epistle.
So sufficiency would have to belong to the whole Canon. Missing books would mean missing doctrine.
They claim many sacred books have perished: Nathan and Gad, Ahijah and Iddo, Solomon's songs and parables, plus a Laodicean letter and perhaps another Corinthian letter.
From today's incomplete Canon, they say, salvation's doctrine cannot be drawn sufficiently.
